function.name: telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get
function.description: Retrieves specified telemetry information for a network interface within a given fabric, node, and pod, filtered by the interface and information types. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

fabricName.description: The name of the fabric to limit the nodes pertaining to the given fabric name.

nodeId.description: The identifier of the node to limit the results pertaining to the given node ID.

podId.description: The identifier of the pod to limit the results pertaining to the given pod ID.

interfaceType.description: The type of the interface to limit the results pertaining to the given interface type.

infoType.description: The type of information to retrieve about the interface.

message.content:
I’m afraid there isn’t a built‑in “get all nodes” helper exposed through the single telemetry function I’ve got access to (`telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get`). That routine pulls **per‑interface** statistics (e.g., interfaces, status, stats, errors) from a *specific* node/pod/interface inside a fabric – it doesn’t return the full list of nodes that belong to a fabric. ### What you’ll usually do instead | Method | Typical usage | |--------|---------------| | **CLI** | On the fabric’s control plane (or a leaf/router), run something like:
`show chassis cluster members`
or
`show system inventory`
This lists every node, its role, serial numbers, firmware versions, etc. | | **REST API** | Most modern fabrics expose a `/api/system/nodes` or similar endpoint.
E.g.: 
curl -k https://23.31.32.1/api/v1/system/nodes

You’d authenticate first (basic auth, token, etc.). | | **SNMP** | Walk OIDs under `.nodes` to enumerate nodes. | If your goal is simply to see what devices exist in the *test‑de* fabric, try: ```bash ssh admin@23.31.32.1 ``` then at the prompt: ```text admin@test-de# show chassis cluster members ``` This will print each member’s hostname/IP, role (leaf/spine/control), uptime, and health state. --- #### Quick reference for the REST route (if your environment supports it) ```bash # Get authentication token (example) TOKEN=$(curl -sk \ -u admin:password \ https://23.31.32.1/api/login | jq -r .token) # Query nodes curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -k https://23.31.32.1/api/v1/system/nodes ``` Replace `admin`, `password`, and the exact URL path according to your vendor’s documentation. --- Let me know if you’re looking for a different kind of detail (firmware version, port counts, etc.)—there might be a more targeted API call or CLI command for that!
